summary:
Bahrain repealed its British colonial-era sodomy statute in 1976 and is the only Gulf state that does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy. The 1976 penal code sets the age of adulthood for consensual same-sex acts at 21, and no statute criminalises transgender expression as such.

Decriminalisation does not prevent arrest. Police apply the morality and indecency provisions of the penal code, Articles 324, 329 and 350, which carry three months to two years' imprisonment, fines of up to 200 Bahraini dinars, and deportation for non-Bahrainis. The government has used these articles against people suspected of being LGBTQI+ or of cross-dressing: in 2009 a man was sentenced to one month in jail for wearing an abaya and carrying a purse in public, and in 2011 police raided a party described as a same-sex wedding.

Entry is a documented exposure point. The Interior Minister stated that suspected, described as effeminate, homosexuals are barred from entering Bahrain through airport checks, and bills tabled for passage proposed to bar LGBTQ foreigners from entry or residency permits. In September 2013 the Gulf Cooperation Council agreed to discuss a proposal to test and exclude gay foreigners, though officials later backtracked. Deportation is an available penalty under the indecency provisions for non-Bahrainis.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are blocked at first instance. In a May 2023 judgment a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare on Islamic Sharia grounds, and refused his request for a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination. Courts require medical documentation of a sex change operation or medical necessity to alter legal gender markers, and a 2023 ruling held sex-reassignment procedures contrary to Islamic law where cases are treated as gender dysphoria alone, confining eligibility to people with intersex traits.

There is no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. Hate speech against LGBTQ people carries no legal consequence, a gap the sources attribute partly to Article 309, which protects religious groups but extends no equivalent protection to LGBTQ people.

No LGBTQ-specific facilities, shelters or community organisations exist. The US Department of State reports no approved LGBTQ-related organisations, and ILGA assesses registration of a sexual- or gender-diversity group as improbable because the body controlling association registration may refuse any group judged contrary to morality or public order.

Article 330 of the penal code requires that anyone charged with prostitution or fujoor be taken to hospital for sexually transmitted disease testing and potentially relocated to a medical facility. A bill proposed in October 2021 would have criminalised promoting or inviting others to homosexual gatherings with up to five years' imprisonment; the status of the pending bills in this record is unresolved.
tangentialFactors:
The Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation in February 2024, and parliamentary hostility to LGBTQ people is an active current rather than a residual feature of the colonial-era code.

False accusations of homosexuality function as a instrument of political pressure. The sources document their use to discredit and bully government critics and protesters, including the human rights advocate Nabeel Rajab and demonstrators at Pearl Square in 2011.

Media treatment compounds official hostility: a widely viewed caricature published by Albilad on 3 August 2024 depicted a pride flag printed on a roll of toilet paper captioned as the correct place for it.

Bahrain's 1976 repeal makes it the only Gulf jurisdiction without an explicit same-sex intimacy offence, so regional comparison overstates the practical gap: arrests here proceed under morality and indecency articles rather than under a sodomy statute.
localsOnly:
Educational policy targets gender and sexuality directly. In response to parliamentary questions about lesbianism in schools, the Assistant Under-Secretary for Educational Services stated that the Education Ministry is not responsible for addressing sexuality, that it is parents' job, and that the public should not make a big deal out of a problem that does not exist, while adding that students whose appearance contradicts school values should be disciplined. A related bill proposed instructing teachers to recognise warning signs of homosexuality or cross-dressing so that children could be punished.

On 14 February 2024 the Ministry of Education referred a private school's administration and its entire board to investigation and dismissed the general manager after a video showed two male students performing a classroom scene in which they pretended to propose to each other. A 2022 incident, in which a private school distributed material perceived as promoting homosexuality, also produced calls for stricter legislation.

Association registration is controlled by a body that may refuse any group judged contrary to morality or public order, which is why the sources treat registration of an LGBTQ organisation as improbable. The US Department of State reports that no LGBTQ-related organisations are approved. The Gulf Daily News has run articles on female homosexuality in girls' high schools.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on the basic legal position and the conflict is unresolved. Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada response RIO BHR105575.E of August 2016, covering 2011 to July 2016, reports that according to sources homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain, citing Canadian and Gulf press material, which contradicts the 1976-decriminalisation reading carried by Wikipedia, Outright International and the 2023 US State Department. This record does not adjudicate between them.

Cairo 52 reports that Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for a decade, including UN human-rights bodies and Amnesty International, so local media often serve as the only source available for this jurisdiction. The age of the sourced material should be read against that access restriction.

No trans-specific violence or killing figures for Bahrain appear in this inventory, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made from these sources, and none is asserted. The enactment status of the pending bills, including the October 2021 proposal, is not established here.
